Sanofi expands Canadians' COVID-19 vaccine choice with availability of Nuvaxovid®for the 2026-2027 respiratory season CNW Group Thu, October 29, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT 5 min read SNY +2.81% SAN -3.59% SNY +2.81% Nuvaxovid®, a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, will be available in 10 provinces and one territory for the fall 2026-2027 respiratory season A protein-based, non-mRNA vaccine that has demonstrated high efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19 in clinical trials Availability underscores Sanofi's commitment to public health and vaccine innovation in Canada TORONTO, Oct. 28, 2026 /CNW/ -- Sanofi Canada is pleased to announce that Nuvaxovid®, a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, will be available in all 10 provinces and the Yukon for the 2026-2027 season through provincial respiratory programs and most private insurers. Sanofi is the largest biopharma manufacturer in Canada, and is investing, innovating and operating across the full life sciences value chain. We are 2,000+ employees strong, invest 20% of our revenue annually in biopharma research, and are on track to deliver over $2 billion in new infrastructure investments by 2028. Sanofi is committed to our community and is working with partners to foster a long-term sustainable ecosystem and build a healthier Canada. Nuvaxovid is currently available in British Columbia, Alberta, and Quebec. In Ontario, it is expected to become available through healthcare provider offices and public health units beginning the week of October 26, 2026, with availability at pharmacies to follow. For information on availability in all provinces, individuals are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, pharmacy, or public health unit in advance to confirm vaccine availability. As a protein-based, non-mRNA option, Nuvaxovid provides Canadians with an additional vaccine option to help protect against COVID-19. As respiratory viruses begin to circulate more widely during the fall and winter months, the availability of both mRNA and non-mRNA, protein-based COVID-19 vaccines supports informed vaccine decision-making based on individual preferences and healthcare provider recommendations. "It's important for Canadians to have choice when it comes to COVID-19 vaccination and for protecting their overall health," said Michael Laclair, General Manager, Canada, Vaccines at Sanofi. "The availability of Nuvaxovid this respiratory season provides Canadians with a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine option backed by strong clinical evidence. We hope that having additional safe and effective vaccine options will encourage more Canadians to get vaccinated and help protect themselves against COVID-19 this season. Nuvaxovid reflects another step in our continued commitment to building a diverse portfolio of best-in-class vaccines to improve lives and build a healthier Canada." COVID‐19 continues to have a significant impact on Canadians, with effects that can extend far beyond the initial infection. During the 2024-2025 respiratory virus season, more than 120,000 COVID‐19 cases, 33,500 hospitalizations and 2,300 deaths were reported across Canada.1 People living with chronic conditions such as heart disease and diabetes may face a higher risk of severe COVID‐19 outcomes.2 Research also suggests that the virus may increase the risk of longer-term cardiovascular complications, including heart attack and stroke.3 Despite these risks, many Canadians remain unprotected with nearly 77% of adults not receiving a COVID‐19 vaccine during the last respiratory season.4 Story Continues Nuvaxovid is indicated for the active immunization against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) virus in individuals 12 years of age and older.5 It has been shown to have a favourable tolerability profile suitable for seasonal vaccination.6,7 The vaccine uses a well-established protein-based technology platform and has also demonstrated efficacy of approximately 90% in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 based on pivotal phase 3 clinical studies.8,9 Vaccine choice is particularly important for the approximately 5 million Canadians aged 15 years or older who live with a compromised immune system that can increase their risk of severe outcomes from COVID-19.10 These individuals are more vulnerable to complications from COVID-19 due to underlying medical conditions or treatments that can weaken the body's immune response.11 "For many immunocompromised Canadians, COVID-19 remains a significant health concern and vaccination continues to play an important role in helping reduce the risk of severe illness," said Michelle Burleigh, Co-chair, Canadian Immunocompromised Advocacy Network (CIAN). "The availability of Nuvaxovid provides another option and reflects the importance of ensuring Canadians have access to a range of vaccine choices that meet their individual needs and circumstances." Nuvaxovid is available through provincial and territorial vaccination programs in participating jurisdictions. Canadians are encouraged to get vaccinated against COVID-19 this season; they can consult their healthcare provider, pharmacist, or local public health authority for information about eligibility and vaccine availability in their region. Healthcare providers and pharmacists can contact their local health authority to obtain more information about Nuvaxovid and how to order it. About Sanofi Sanofi is an R&D driven, AI-powered biopharma company committed to improving people's lives and delivering compelling growth. We apply our deep understanding of the immune system to invent medicines and vaccines that treat and protect millions of people around the world, with an innovative pipeline that could benefit millions more. Sanofi is the largest biopharma manufacturer in Canada, and is investing, innovating and operating across the full life sciences value chain. We are 2,000+ employees strong, invest 20% of our revenue annually in biopharma research, and are on track to deliver over $2 billion in new infrastructure investments by 2028. Sanofi is committed to our community and is working with partners to foster a long-term sustainable ecosystem and build a healthier Canada. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Orbital inflammatory pseudotumor cases rose during COVID-19 Omicron wave by October 30, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Orbital inflammatory pseudotumor cases rose during COVID-19 Omicron wave Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Patients presenting with orbital disease at one hospital during the peak of the COVID-19 Omicron wave were markedly more likely to have orbital inflammatory pseudotumor than those seen in the same months of the previous three years, according to a clinical case analysis published in BMC Ophthalmology. Of 62 patients diagnosed with orbital diseases from December 2022 to January 2023, 13 cases, or 20.97 percent, involved orbital inflammatory pseudotumor, a proportion the authors report as significantly higher than in the control group drawn from the corresponding periods of the preceding three years. The study used the abbreviation OIP for orbital inflammatory pseudotumor. The researchers set out to compare the proportion of OIP among orbital disease cases during the Omicron peak with earlier years and to describe the clinical features of OIP in patients with recent COVID-19 infection. The study group comprised the 62 orbital disease patients seen during the two-month wave period, while the control group consisted of OIP patients from the same months in the previous three years, allowing a direct seasonal comparison. Discover more Get Rapid Tests Read Health News Study Anatomy The 13 OIP cases showed a consistent pattern of single-eye involvement. Six occurred in the right eye and seven in the left eye, with no apparent preference between the two sides. Eight patients were male and five were female, a slight male predominance, and ages ranged from 16 to 65, with the authors characterizing the condition as showing middle-aged prevalence in this cohort. Discover more Order Contacts Read Med Journals Find Treatments COVID-19 All cases had acute onset clinical features. Eyelid swelling and conjunctival hyperemia with chemosis were each present in 61.54 percent of patients, making them the most common signs. Ocular motility disorders affected 53.85 percent, while eye pain and diplopia each occurred in 46.15 percent. Less frequent findings included proptosis in 23.08 percent, ptosis in 15.38 percent, and decreased vision in 7.69 percent. The reported features included eyelid swelling, conjunctival hyperemia and chemosis, ocular motility disorders, eye pain, diplopia, proptosis, ptosis, and decreased vision. OIP was confirmed through ocular ultrasound, orbital CT, and MRI scans. The study reported that glucocorticoid therapy resulted in excellent treatment outcomes. Summarizing their findings, the researchers report that the proportion of OIP among orbital disease cases presenting to their hospital increased significantly from December 2022 to January 2023 compared with the corresponding periods of the preceding three years. They describe the condition in this setting as featuring single-eye onset, no significant difference between the eyes, a slightly higher incidence rate in males than females, and middle-aged prevalence, with acute onset symptoms including eyelid swelling, conjunctival hyperemia and chemosis, ocular motility disorders, and eye pain. The authors are careful to flag the limits of the evidence. The study group was relatively small, they write, and it requires further research to provide more reliable evidence. The study group consisted of 62 patients diagnosed with orbital diseases at one hospital from December 2022 to January 2023, and the control group comprised OIP patients from the same months in the previous 3 years. The authors note that the study group was relatively small and that further research is required to provide more reliable evidence. content_title: Covid-19: Still a risk that needs to be treated quickly
content: (Photo credit: SDI Productions/Getty Images) Much of the world may want COVID-19 to remain squarely in our collective rear-view mirror, but the virus — several years after initial outbreaks and treatment development — is still with us and a threat. While vaccines helped reduce severe outcomes during the pandemic, their use has declined. But the virus remains a serious threat to the people most vulnerable to it, experts warn. 1 Older people with underlying conditions remain most at risk for severe health outcomes, putting the residents of long-term care and skilled-nursing facilities in a particularly tenuous position. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 The mild illness today doesn’t predict the mild illness on day seven in this population. It’s a cascading problem. Stefan Gravenstein, MD, Brown University’s Schools of Medicine and Public Health The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates there are still millions of cases each year in the United States, hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations, and tens of thousands of deaths. 6 It’s estimated that residents of long-term care facilities account for 1 in 5 hospitalized adults older than 65 with COVID-19. 1 Further, studies have concluded that a COVID-19 infection may lead to adverse long-term health outcomes, including new-onset, heart failure, diabetes, asthma, and COPD, as well as increasing the likelihood of suffering major adverse cardiovascular events, strokes, and kidney injuries. 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 That’s why a team of doctors from Brown University wants long-term care operators and administrators to know that there are chances to intervene, to help prevent some of the worst results — if they act early enough. The clinical experts discussed the challenges and explained the steps that can be taken to mitigate potential problems during a recent McKnight’s webinar entitled, “Expert perspectives on closing the COVID-19 treatment gap in long-term care.” The team’s Health Advancement Antiviral Treatment for Long-Term Care (HEAL-LTC) program, sponsored by Pfizer, identified barriers to early intervention and has crafted tools for operators and their caretaking staffs to act sooner. “The challenge we have is that everybody thinks they know what’s going to happen if they just have the sniffles. But, in fact, the sniffles may just be the first sign,” said Stefan Gravenstein, MD, with Brown University’s Schools of Medicine and Public Health. (Photo credit: Pekic/Getty Images) Five days to act The key is to get started at the time of admission. ... Families generally just want more information. Barbara Resnick, PhD, University of Maryland School of Nursing It can take four to six days for mild symptoms to show themselves. 13 , 14 Shortness of breath and other pulmonary responses can take five to eight days. 15 , 16 , 17 Worse symptoms — the kind that can send people to the hospital and ICU for hyperinflammation — can take eight to 12 days. 13,16, 18 For that reason, the medical community has settled on a five-day window, with the clock starting at the first sign of symptoms, to effectively treat COVID-19 with oral antivirals where appropriate. Outside that five-day window, it may be too late for a treatment to make a difference. That leaves a limited amount of time to call a family member, to obtain the medication, to make dose adjustments, and more. Gravenstein likened it to a “fire drill.” Investigating hurdles to early intervention The Brown University team started its investigation by surveying 18 long-term care professionals working at four facilities across Rhode Island and interviewing five of them. All participants were directly involved with prescribing, dispensing, administering, or overseeing medication use in the facilities. Several challenges to early intervention became apparent. Early symptoms such as fatigue, confusion, and falls are common among long-term care residents. A caretaker might attribute the symptoms to some other ailment, losing critical time to treat. The time it takes to secure a family’s consent can shrink the window of treatment, not because the family is unreachable but because the urgency of the situation isn’t communicated clearly enough. The complexity of prescribing the antiviral based on other possible drug interactions and side effects and the need for alternative dosing if a resident can’t swallow pills takes time to work through if not done in advance. Preparations for ready access to medication, especially late at night or on a weekend, are often not put in place beforehand. That’s all on top of entirely reasonable pandemic fatigue leading to undertreatment of mild illnesses, as well as polypharmacy concerns and false reassurance if a resident had the virus before and did fine without treatment. The team, which included Brown University’s Rosa Baier, MPH, with the School of Public Health, and Yasin Abul, MD, with the School of Medicine, conducted a needs assessment, developing practical tools to address those needs and sharing them with two facilities to gain feedback. (Photo credit: supersizer/Getty Images) Early intervention before any symptoms The team’s resulting initiative urges that one of the first steps be taken months ahead of any possible diagnosis. Gaining the consent of a resident’s family can come as early as admission or any moment in advance when the need is less urgent. A brief family caregiver handout developed by the Brown University team, written in plain language, explains to the resident’s family why the first five days from the onset of symptoms are so critical to act. In frail adult residents, COVID rarely looks like COVID, per se. Yasin Abul, MD, Brown University School of Medicine “The key here is to get started at the time of admission,” said Barbara Resnick, PhD, RN, with the University of Maryland School of Nursing. It’s a calm time to give them options and have a discussion when there isn’t an ensuing crisis. “What the project detailed is that families generally just want more information.” The form also answers frequently asked questions, including what the adverse effects might be or why a resident would need treatment if they’ve received the vaccine. It is during these conversations that the facility can gain consent and keep it on file, at the ready for when treatment is ultimately needed. At that time, the facility’s caregivers can reach out to family to update them on the situation with consent already in hand. Staying within the treatment window By the time symptoms show up, the primary challenge is recognizing whether a resident has COVID or not, which isn’t as simple as it sounds. “In frail adult residents, COVID rarely looks like COVID, per se,” said Dr. Abul. To help, the team developed a one-page guide for nurses that has advice for signs to watch for. The “Spot It & Act Fast” guide notes several symptoms: new confusion, unexpected falls, poor oral intake, unusual sleepiness, loose stools, or family members saying the resident hasn’t been themselves. Abul knows that new confusion and falls might be mistaken for a urinary tract infection. In both cases, he urges caretakers to test for a UTI and for COVID, not one or the other. In other words, assume it’s COVID and let the provider rule it out, he said. The next step is communicating with the prescriber. A one-page Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation (or SBAR) document guides nurses in a script and decision path for when they call the medical provider, ensuring they’ve already gathered all the necessary information. Depending on what the provider decides, the guide also includes different outcomes as well as language a nurse could use to gain more clarity on why a treatment decision was made. “That call on Friday night at 9 p.m. can be so stressful for that nurse because she knows the person answering on the other end may not be so nice,” said Resnick. Finally, the team also highly encourages facilities to establish a routine workflow in advance that includes plans for having or accessing tests quickly and plans for obtaining the medicine overnight or on a weekend, as well as any known interaction concerns. Ed Davidson, PharmD, cofounder, chairman, and chief of strategy with Insight Therapeutics, reminded operators that there’s room to plan ahead for when an interaction shows up. Interactions with antivirals may be addressed by a temporary adjustment or a brief hold. “If that’s already discussed and worked out ahead of time, it lets the provider act within the treatment window instead of getting stalled,” he noted. Speedy treatment via prepped workflow The result of the team’s discussions and assessments with facility professionals is a clear pathway for treatment, helping to ensure that the treatment is made before it’s too late. They noted: It starts with providing the resident’s family easy-to-navigate information and gaining their consent for treatment. Next, it involves nurses and facility staff spotting COVID-19 symptoms and acting fast. Then, in calling the provider for their decision to treat or not, a nurse can be sure they have all the necessary information in advance and stick to a script in case they’re uncertain about communicating the resident’s needs. Finally, if following the recommended workflow, including knowing where and how to obtain the needed medicine for treatment, they will be able to treat the illness within the five-day window. Dr. Abul envisions success this way: A nurse notices a resident is a little off. The nurse tests the resident right away, then calls the provider within the hour, providing all the needed information as laid out with the SBAR-driven script. “The family already knows what’s going on because we already talked about it at admission at the beginning of care planning,” he said. Then, it’s simply a matter of getting the first dose administered in a timely manner. “All it is, is workflow.” Acting fast also determines whether COVID-19 may or may not spread among the rest of the facility’s residents. “The mild illness today doesn’t predict the mild illness on day seven in this population,” emphasized Gravenstein. “It’s a cascading problem.” ■ Havers F. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health SARS-CoV-2 antibodies found in up to 76 percent of people across three West African countries by October 27, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 SARS-CoV-2 antibodies found in up to 76 percent of people across three West African countries Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A large community-based serosurvey spanning Burkina Faso, Ghana and Nigeria has found that between 24.1 percent and 76.4 percent of participants carried IgG antibodies against SARS-CoV-2, indicating that exposure to the virus was far more widespread in West African communities than officially reported case counts during the pandemic had suggested. The study, published in Frontiers in Public Health, recruited 20,748 participants across the three countries and is described by its authors as one of the largest multi-country community-based SARS-CoV-2 seroepidemiology studies conducted in Africa to date. The research was designed to address a puzzle that had persisted since the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic. Africa appeared to have experienced low SARS-CoV-2 infection rates and comparatively low COVID-19 morbidity and mortality, at least as measured by reported cases and deaths. Several earlier studies, however, had reported high levels of SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity among apparently healthy Africans, a discrepancy that raised two competing explanations. One possibility was that the virus had indeed spread extensively through African populations while causing relatively little severe clinical disease. The other, advanced by some researchers, was that apparent seropositivity could have resulted from pre-existing cross-reactive antibodies, antibodies raised against other coronaviruses or related pathogens that happen to bind in SARS-CoV-2 tests without reflecting true infection. To track exposure trends over time, the research teams conducted cross-sectional surveys at study sites conveniently selected within each of the three countries. Sampling was carried out during two distinct phases of the pandemic: the period when the Delta variant was dominant and the period when the Omicron variant was dominant, both nationally and globally. Discover more Study Biology Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Read Med Journals Check Symptoms Because the investigators did not perform widespread viral sequencing on participant samples, they could not attribute any individual's seropositivity to infection with a specific variant. Instead, they classified the sampling periods by whichever variant was reported as dominant at the time the samples were collected, an important methodological limitation that shapes how the results should be interpreted. Antibody detection relied on rapid diagnostic tests that measure two classes of immunoglobulins. The teams used SARS-CoV-2 IgG/IgM rapid diagnostic tests from Prestige Diagnostics at the sites in Ghana and Burkina Faso, and kits from SD Biosensor at the sites in Nigeria. These immunoassay kits had published validation procedures, and the researchers describe them as validated for the purpose of detecting SARS-CoV-2 antibodies in peripheral blood. The primary outcome of the study was the proportion of each sampled population with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, a standard measure in seroepidemiology known as seroprevalence. In addition to blood sampling, participants' demographic and clinical data were collected using a semi-structured questionnaire. This allowed the investigators to examine how seropositivity related to factors such as age and other demographic characteristics, and to record participants' vaccination status and attitudes. The headline result was the wide range of IgG seropositivity across sites, from 24.1 percent at the lowest to 76.4 percent at the highest, with higher rates observed during the Omicron-dominant period than during the Delta-dominant period. What the data do establish is that the fraction of community members with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies grew substantially between the two sampling windows across the study populations. A crucial contextual finding concerns vaccination. All study sites showed low self-reported vaccination rates, which the authors say suggests that the observed seropositivity was primarily driven by natural infection rather than by vaccine-induced antibodies. Discover more COVID-19 Read Health News Find Treatments Book Lab Tests Track Outbreaks The demographic analysis revealed a consistent pattern for age and a heterogeneous one for other factors. Across all sites, there was a significant positive association between seropositivity and age, meaning older participants were more likely to carry SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies. By contrast, the associations between seropositivity and other demographic factors were country-dependent, differing between Burkina Faso, Ghana and Nigeria. Taken together, the findings support what the authors describe as a marked disconnect between high population exposure and low reported clinical burden in the region. The study as summarized cannot adjudicate between these possibilities, since it measured antibody prevalence rather than disease outcomes, and its sites were conveniently rather than randomly selected within each country, which limits how precisely the results can be generalized to national populations. The authors argue that their results underscore the need for strengthened community-based surveillance in West Africa. SANOFI Oct 29, 2026, 07:30 ET Share this article Share this article Nuvaxovid®, a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, will be available in 10 provinces and one territory for the fall 2026-2027 respiratory season A protein-based, non-mRNA vaccine that has demonstrated high efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19 in clinical trials Availability underscores Sanofi's commitment to public health and vaccine innovation in Canada TORONTO, Oct. 28, 2026 /CNW/ -- Sanofi Canada is pleased to announce that Nuvaxovid®, a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, will be available in all 10 provinces and the Yukon for the 2026-2027 season through provincial respiratory programs and most private insurers. Nuvaxovid is currently available in British Columbia, Alberta, and Quebec. In Ontario, it is expected to become available through healthcare provider offices and public health units beginning the week of October 26, 2026, with availability at pharmacies to follow. For information on availability in all provinces, individuals are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, pharmacy, or public health unit in advance to confirm vaccine availability. As a protein-based, non-mRNA option, Nuvaxovid provides Canadians with an additional vaccine option to help protect against COVID-19. As respiratory viruses begin to circulate more widely during the fall and winter months, the availability of both mRNA and non-mRNA, protein-based COVID-19 vaccines supports informed vaccine decision-making based on individual preferences and healthcare provider recommendations. "It's important for Canadians to have choice when it comes to COVID-19 vaccination and for protecting their overall health," said Michael Laclair, General Manager, Canada, Vaccines at Sanofi. "The availability of Nuvaxovid this respiratory season provides Canadians with a protein-based, non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccine option backed by strong clinical evidence. We hope that having additional safe and effective vaccine options will encourage more Canadians to get vaccinated and help protect themselves against COVID-19 this season. Nuvaxovid reflects another step in our continued commitment to building a diverse portfolio of best-in-class vaccines to improve lives and build a healthier Canada." COVID‐19 continues to have a significant impact on Canadians, with effects that can extend far beyond the initial infection. During the 2024-2025 respiratory virus season, more than 120,000 COVID‐19 cases, 33,500 hospitalizations and 2,300 deaths were reported across Canada.1 People living with chronic conditions such as heart disease and diabetes may face a higher risk of severe COVID‐19 outcomes.2 Research also suggests that the virus may increase the risk of longer-term cardiovascular complications, including heart attack and stroke.3 Despite these risks, many Canadians remain unprotected with nearly 77% of adults not receiving a COVID‐19 vaccine during the last respiratory season.4 Nuvaxovid is indicated for the active immunization against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) virus in individuals 12 years of age and older.5 It has been shown to have a favourable tolerability profile suitable for seasonal vaccination.6,7 The vaccine uses a well-established protein-based technology platform and has also demonstrated efficacy of approximately 90% in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 based on pivotal phase 3 clinical studies.8,9 Vaccine choice is particularly important for the approximately 5 million Canadians aged 15 years or older who live with a compromised immune system that can increase their risk of severe outcomes from COVID-19.10 These individuals are more vulnerable to complications from COVID-19 due to underlying medical conditions or treatments that can weaken the body's immune response.11 "For many immunocompromised Canadians, COVID-19 remains a significant health concern and vaccination continues to play an important role in helping reduce the risk of severe illness," said Michelle Burleigh, Co-chair, Canadian Immunocompromised Advocacy Network (CIAN). "The availability of Nuvaxovid provides another option and reflects the importance of ensuring Canadians have access to a range of vaccine choices that meet their individual needs and circumstances." Nuvaxovid is available through provincial and territorial vaccination programs in participating jurisdictions. Canadians are encouraged to get vaccinated against COVID-19 this season; they can consult their healthcare provider, pharmacist, or local public health authority for information about eligibility and vaccine availability in their region. Healthcare providers and pharmacists can contact their local health authority to obtain more information about Nuvaxovid and how to order it. About Sanofi Sanofi is an R&D driven, AI-powered biopharma company committed to improving people's lives and delivering compelling growth. We apply our deep understanding of the immune system to invent medicines and vaccines that treat and protect millions of people around the world, with an innovative pipeline that could benefit millions more. Sanofi is the largest biopharma manufacturer in Canada, and is investing, innovating and operating across the full life sciences value chain. We are 2,000+ employees strong, invest 20% of our revenue annually in biopharma research, and are on track to deliver over $2 billion in new infrastructure investments by 2028. Sanofi is committed to our community and is working with partners to foster a long-term sustainable ecosystem and build a healthier Canada. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Synthetic Sulfolipid Reshapes Dendritic Cell Response to SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein in Lab Model by October 29, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Synthetic Sulfolipid Reshapes Dendritic Cell Response to SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein in Lab Model Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A synthetic sulfolipid called Sulfavant A can reprogram how human dendritic cells respond to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in laboratory cultures, taming the inflammatory molecules the virus normally provokes while steering T cells toward regulatory and helper fates, according to a new study published in the journal Discover Immunity. The work, conducted entirely in vitro with cells from healthy donors, offers a detailed picture of an unconventional immune-activation pathway that its investigators say could eventually inform therapies for hyperinflammation, although the authors themselves caution that dampening early antiviral responses remains a real risk and that animal and clinical validation will be essential before any translational application. Sulfavant A is a synthetic glycolipid developed as a prototype for a family of small molecules that activate dendritic cells without triggering the classical inflammatory cascade. Earlier work by the same group showed that the compound engages TREM2, the triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2, and drives dendritic cell maturation characterized by upregulation of surface costimulatory molecules in the absence of inflammatory markers and cytokine release. When the engagement of TREM2 is impaired, the dendritic cell response to Sulfavant A is reduced. The researchers describe this profile as distinct from the inflammatory paradigm induced by pattern recognition receptors, the sensors such as toll-like receptors that typically ignite antiviral and inflammatory programs. The new experiments focused on a gap in that earlier picture: whether the compound could act against a viral antigen capable of evading antigen-presenting cell recognition and suppressing adaptive effector functions. The team used human monocyte-derived dendritic cells generated from peripheral blood of healthy volunteers at Umberto I Hospital of Nocera Inferiore in Salerno, Italy. Seven donor samples were used to reach statistically meaningful results, and the only exclusion criterion was prior COVID-19 vaccination, so the donors were unvaccinated at the time of blood collection. Monocytes were isolated with magnetic beads to a purity of at least 98 percent and cultured for six days with interleukin-4 and GM-CSF to yield immature dendritic cells. To mimic viral exposure, the researchers treated the cells with a commercial pool of lyophilized peptides spanning the immunodominant sequence domains of the spike glycoprotein, referred to throughout the study as SPIKE. This pool includes the receptor-binding domain, the region of the spike protein that engages the ACE2 receptor on host cells and is known to activate dendritic cells and promote their maturation. As specificity controls, parallel cultures received peptide pools covering the complete sequences of the viral membrane glycoprotein and the nucleocapsid phosphoprotein; neither of these produced measurable effects on the dendritic cells, supporting the view that the observed activity was specific to spike. After 24 hours of treatment, the contrast between the two conditions was stark. Spike peptides alone elicited minimal changes in costimulatory marker expression but markedly induced secretion of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha, the two cytokines that define the inflammatory signature of clinical SARS-CoV-2 infection. When Sulfavant A was co-administered with the spike peptides, the compound significantly upregulated the costimulatory molecules CD86, CD83, ICOSL and OX40L while reducing interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha back to basal levels. Spike stimulation did not affect HLA-DR expression, did not induce the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10 in the monocultures, and left interleukin-12 and interleukin-1 beta unchanged. The team then asked whether these dendritic cell changes would translate into altered T cell behavior. In autologous co-cultures, dendritic cells were pre-loaded with spike peptides in the presence or absence of Sulfavant A for 24 hours, the stimulus was washed away, and naive T cells from the same donor were added at a one-to-ten dendritic cell to T cell ratio. After 48 hours, the combination treatment sustained upregulation of ICOSL and OX40L, whereas spike alone selectively enhanced expression of MHC class I, CD40 and the checkpoint inhibitory molecule PD-L1, effects that Sulfavant A counteracted and restored to basal levels. Interleukin-6 secretion, elevated by spike alone, was again significantly reduced by the co-treatment, and an increase in HLA-DR was observed under the combined condition. After seven days of co-culture, proliferation measured by CFSE dilution showed that spike alone induced proliferation of CD8-positive T cells compared with untreated cultures, a response that was significantly attenuated in the presence of Sulfavant A. The compound instead promoted proliferation of a distinct CD4-positive T cell subset, and interleukin-2 was detected exclusively in the supernatants of samples treated with spike together with Sulfavant A. Flow cytometry of T cell subpopulations revealed no significant differences in Th1 or Th2 markers, but the combination expanded two defined lineages: peripheral regulatory T cells with the phenotype CD127-negative, CD4-positive, CD25-positive and FOXP3-positive, accompanied by increased interleukin-10 in the supernatants, and T follicular helper cells marked by CXCR5, BCL6 and interleukin-21, accompanied by a significant rise in interleukin-21 secretion. Cell clustering between dendritic cells and lymphocytes, a phenomenon previously associated with regulatory T cell interactions, was also evident under the combined condition. The authors interpret these results as evidence that Sulfavant A, in the presence of spike protein, promotes polarization toward both regulatory T cells and T follicular helper cells. The follicular helper lineage, mainly represented in the germinal centers of lymph nodes, is critical for activating B lymphocytes and driving antibody production, and growing evidence links this population to protective immunity induced by vaccines and to long-term protection from SARS-CoV-2. However, the researchers did not directly assess whether the expanded follicular helper cells functionally enhance B cell activation, noting that this lay beyond the scope of the study and that future investigations are planned to confirm whether the polarization translates into enhanced B cell help and antibody responses. Several important limitations frame these findings. All conclusions derive from analyses of total naive T cell populations in vitro rather than enumerated antigen-specific clones, so the results reflect population-level T cell responsiveness rather than direct evidence of spike specificity, even though the use of autologous dendritic cells pulsed with a defined viral antigen makes an antigen-driven component plausible. The study also did not directly demonstrate TREM2 dependence in this experimental setting; the observed profile is consistent with the earlier biochemical evidence that Sulfavant A binds TREM2, but other receptors or pathways may contribute, and loss-of-function studies will be required to establish the mechanism. The spike protein is known to engage TLR2 and TLR4 on myeloid cells and trigger inflammatory signaling, and the authors suggest that TREM2’s downstream pathway through DAP12, SYK and PI3K, which inhibits proinflammatory cytokine release, may contribute to the immunomodulatory effects, though this remains to be defined. The dual nature of the intervention is a recurring theme in the paper. On one hand, the reduction of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha, together with restored costimulatory signaling and a shift toward CD4-positive T cell proliferation, suggests a potential role in mitigating the immune-related adverse events of uncontrolled inflammation while preserving regulatory and helper T cell functions, with envisioned contexts ranging from vaccine adjuvants to severe COVID-19 and post-acute sequelae. On the other hand, the same regulatory activity that restrains immunopathology also reduced CD8-positive T cell expansion, and the authors acknowledge that Treg polarization and regulatory ligand expression on dendritic cells could have constrained antiviral effector functions and potentially impacted viral clearance. At present, the results are limited to in vitro models, and the researchers state that careful in vivo validation will be essential to determine whether the net effect of Sulfavant A is beneficial in specific clinical contexts. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses by October 30, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A new serological study reports that acute SARS-CoV-2 infection rapidly raises antibody levels not only against the pandemic virus but also against the seasonal human coronaviruses that cause common colds. The finding, published in the journal Discover Viruses, adds to evidence that the immune response to SARS-CoV-2 departs from the classical antibody trajectory, in which immunoglobulin M appears first before the body class-switches to immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin A. That atypical pattern, the authors argue, complicates the long-standing practice of using IgM as a marker of recent infection. The research team, led by Guadalein Tanunliong and colleagues at the British Columbia public health laboratory network, analyzed serum samples from 51 people with nucleic acid amplification test-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, collected between 0 and 14 days after symptom onset, and compared them with 30 pre-pandemic control samples collected before COVID-19 first appeared in British Columbia, Canada. All 51 infected participants were tested for IgA and IgM, while 26 of the 51 available samples were also tested for IgG. The infected individuals were hospitalized patients with a median age of 68 years, and the study was conducted under a provincial mandate to validate SARS-CoV-2 serological assays for outbreak investigations and seroprevalence work. The investigators used a multiplex immunoassay, the V-PLEX Coronavirus Panel 2 from Meso Scale Discovery, to quantify antibodies against the spike proteins of the four endemic human coronaviruses, HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63, HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-OC43, as well as against the spike, nucleocapsid and receptor binding domain of ancestral SARS-CoV-2. Serum specimens were diluted 1:5000 and run on multi-spot plates with isotype-specific detection antibodies, and seropositivity thresholds were interpreted relative to validated signal cut-off values. The four endemic coronaviruses have circulated in humans since the 1960s, two of alpha lineage and two of beta lineage, and typically reinfect people every two to three years, so antibodies against them often persist at detectable levels throughout life. Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Get Allergy Relief Get Rapid Tests The results confirmed that the antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 starts early and moves fast. Serum collected at both 0 to 7 days and 8 to 14 days after onset showed higher IgA, IgG and IgM levels against SARS-CoV-2 spike, receptor binding domain and nucleocapsid than the pre-pandemic controls, with statistically significant differences. Levels trended higher at 8 to 14 days than at 0 to 7 days across all three isotypes, with the difference reaching statistical significance for IgM. Percent seropositivity also climbed over time: at 0 to 7 days, IgA seropositivity ranged from 73 to 82 percent, slightly above IgG at 56 to 78 percent and IgM at 58 to 76 percent, while by 8 to 14 days IgG seropositivity reached 100 percent for all three SARS-CoV-2 targets, exceeding IgM rates of 83 percent for nucleocapsid and 94 percent for spike and receptor binding domain. The cross-reactive signal emerged most clearly for the beta-lineage seasonal coronaviruses, HCoV-OC43 and HCoV-HKU1. IgM, IgA and IgG antibodies against these two viruses were elevated in infected individuals compared with pre-pandemic controls. At 0 to 7 days, IgM against HCoV-OC43 and IgG against HCoV-HKU1 were already significantly higher in the infected group, while other isotypes trended higher without reaching significance. By 8 to 14 days, all three isotypes against both beta coronaviruses were significantly higher in cases than controls. In contrast, most IgA and IgG responses against the alpha-lineage viruses HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63 were not significantly different between groups, although IgM against HCoV-NL63 was significantly elevated at both time points. To probe the association further, the team stratified infected individuals by their early SARS-CoV-2 antibody status. Among the 13 people who were seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 spike IgG at 0 to 7 days, the so-called early IgG responders, spike IgG levels correlated positively with IgG levels against the beta coronaviruses, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.62 for HCoV-HKU1 and 0.81 for HCoV-OC43. Among the 5 early IgG non-responders, only HCoV-NL63 showed a significant correlation, and it was negative. The authors describe these analyses as exploratory, given the small subgroup sizes, but the pattern is consistent with the idea that a rapid early IgG response to SARS-CoV-2 may reflect recall of humoral memory from prior exposure to related seasonal coronaviruses. IgM showed a parallel cross-reactive association. Among all 51 individuals tested for IgM, high SARS-CoV-2 spike IgM correlated positively with IgM against the seasonal coronavirus spike proteins during acute infection. At 0 to 7 days after onset, the correlation coefficients were highest for HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-NL63, each at 0.76, followed by HCoV-229E at 0.49 and HCoV-OC43 at 0.45. Similar correlations held at 8 to 14 days, with the exception of HCoV-OC43, which did not correlate significantly at that later window. Linear regression models for the infected groups explained a moderate share of the variability, with R-squared values between 0.21 and 0.59, and were generally stronger at 0 to 7 days for HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-NL63. Among pre-pandemic controls, by contrast, no correlation between seasonal coronavirus IgM and SARS-CoV-2 IgM was observed. Discover more Find Lung Care Study Anatomy COVID-19 Read Health News Uninterruptible power supplies An exploratory comparison of IgM to IgG ratios reinforced the picture of an IgG-dominated early response to SARS-CoV-2. Infected individuals showed significantly lower IgM:IgG ratios against SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid and spike than controls, as early as 0 to 7 days after infection, and no significant shift in the ratios occurred between the two time windows. For the seasonal coronaviruses, anti-spike IgM:IgG ratios showed no significant differences between infected individuals and controls, remaining uniformly low for HCoV-229E, HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-OC43. The exception was HCoV-NL63, where the IgM:IgG ratio was elevated in infected individuals, reaching statistical significance at 8 to 14 days, mirroring the elevated IgM levels against that virus. The study also documented baseline cross-reactivity in the pre-pandemic controls. No pre-pandemic seropositivity was observed for SARS-CoV-2 spike for any isotype, but the controls did show seropositivity for the receptor binding domain, at 17 percent for IgG, 10 percent for IgA and 13 percent for IgM, and low-level seropositivity for nucleocapsid in 3 percent for IgA and IgG. The authors note that the receptor binding domain is a smaller protein that yields lower signals and lower positivity thresholds, increasing the likelihood of false positives, and that pre-pandemic cross-reactivity rates can vary with age, year and region. The authors are careful about what the findings do and do not show. The cohort consisted of unvaccinated individuals infected with ancestral SARS-CoV-2, which the authors describe as a valuable reference point for defining early antibody kinetics without confounding from vaccination or reinfection, but the sample was small, drawn largely from hospitalized cases, and lacked clinical data on severity, comorbidities and sex-stratified analyses. There were no paired specimens for individual-level longitudinal follow-up, and the assay measured antibody quantities rather than function, so the cross-reactivity cannot be tied to neutralization or protection. The authors also cannot determine whether the early seasonal coronavirus responses reflect true antibody cross-reactivity or recall of conserved epitopes from prior exposures. Even so, they conclude that the early IgG, IgA and IgM responses to SARS-CoV-2 were associated with seasonal coronavirus responses, supporting earlier pandemic reports that IgM-based tests for recent infection are unreliable for SARS-CoV-2, and underscoring the importance of accounting for cross-reactivity when interpreting serological assays and assessing correlates of protection. C., Krajden, M., Morshed, M., Jassem, A. N., & Sekirov, I. (2026). Cross-reactive IgM, IgA, and IgG antibody responses to seasonal human coronaviruses following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection. title: Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses

content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses by October 30, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Early SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers cross-reactive antibodies against seasonal coronaviruses Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A new serological study reports that acute SARS-CoV-2 infection rapidly raises antibody levels not only against the pandemic virus but also against the seasonal human coronaviruses that cause common colds. The finding, published in the journal Discover Viruses, adds to evidence that the immune response to SARS-CoV-2 departs from the classical antibody trajectory, in which immunoglobulin M appears first before the body class-switches to immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin A. That atypical pattern, the authors argue, complicates the long-standing practice of using IgM as a marker of recent infection. The research team, led by Guadalein Tanunliong and colleagues at the British Columbia public health laboratory network, analyzed serum samples from 51 people with nucleic acid amplification test-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, collected between 0 and 14 days after symptom onset, and compared them with 30 pre-pandemic control samples collected before COVID-19 first appeared in British Columbia, Canada. All 51 infected participants were tested for IgA and IgM, while 26 of the 51 available samples were also tested for IgG. The infected individuals were hospitalized patients with a median age of 68 years, and the study was conducted under a provincial mandate to validate SARS-CoV-2 serological assays for outbreak investigations and seroprevalence work. The investigators used a multiplex immunoassay, the V-PLEX Coronavirus Panel 2 from Meso Scale Discovery, to quantify antibodies against the spike proteins of the four endemic human coronaviruses, HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63, HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-OC43, as well as against the spike, nucleocapsid and receptor binding domain of ancestral SARS-CoV-2. Serum specimens were diluted 1:5000 and run on multi-spot plates with isotype-specific detection antibodies, and seropositivity thresholds were interpreted relative to validated signal cut-off values. The four endemic coronaviruses have circulated in humans since the 1960s, two of alpha lineage and two of beta lineage, and typically reinfect people every two to three years, so antibodies against them often persist at detectable levels throughout life. The results confirmed that the antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 starts early and moves fast. Serum collected at both 0 to 7 days and 8 to 14 days after onset showed higher IgA, IgG and IgM levels against SARS-CoV-2 spike, receptor binding domain and nucleocapsid than the pre-pandemic controls, with statistically significant differences. Levels trended higher at 8 to 14 days than at 0 to 7 days across all three isotypes, with the difference reaching statistical significance for IgM. Percent seropositivity also climbed over time: at 0 to 7 days, IgA seropositivity ranged from 73 to 82 percent, slightly above IgG at 56 to 78 percent and IgM at 58 to 76 percent, while by 8 to 14 days IgG seropositivity reached 100 percent for all three SARS-CoV-2 targets, exceeding IgM rates of 83 percent for nucleocapsid and 94 percent for spike and receptor binding domain. The cross-reactive signal emerged most clearly for the beta-lineage seasonal coronaviruses, HCoV-OC43 and HCoV-HKU1. IgM, IgA and IgG antibodies against these two viruses were elevated in infected individuals compared with pre-pandemic controls. At 0 to 7 days, IgM against HCoV-OC43 and IgG against HCoV-HKU1 were already significantly higher in the infected group, while other isotypes trended higher without reaching significance. By 8 to 14 days, all three isotypes against both beta coronaviruses were significantly higher in cases than controls. In contrast, most IgA and IgG responses against the alpha-lineage viruses HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63 were not significantly different between groups, although IgM against HCoV-NL63 was significantly elevated at both time points. To probe the association further, the team stratified infected individuals by their early SARS-CoV-2 antibody status. Among the 13 people who were seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 spike IgG at 0 to 7 days, the so-called early IgG responders, spike IgG levels correlated positively with IgG levels against the beta coronaviruses, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.62 for HCoV-HKU1 and 0.81 for HCoV-OC43. Among the 5 early IgG non-responders, only HCoV-NL63 showed a significant correlation, and it was negative. The authors describe these analyses as exploratory, given the small subgroup sizes, but the pattern is consistent with the idea that a rapid early IgG response to SARS-CoV-2 may reflect recall of humoral memory from prior exposure to related seasonal coronaviruses. IgM showed a parallel cross-reactive association. Among all 51 individuals tested for IgM, high SARS-CoV-2 spike IgM correlated positively with IgM against the seasonal coronavirus spike proteins during acute infection. At 0 to 7 days after onset, the correlation coefficients were highest for HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-NL63, each at 0.76, followed by HCoV-229E at 0.49 and HCoV-OC43 at 0.45. Similar correlations held at 8 to 14 days, with the exception of HCoV-OC43, which did not correlate significantly at that later window. Linear regression models for the infected groups explained a moderate share of the variability, with R-squared values between 0.21 and 0.59, and were generally stronger at 0 to 7 days for HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-NL63. Among pre-pandemic controls, by contrast, no correlation between seasonal coronavirus IgM and SARS-CoV-2 IgM was observed. An exploratory comparison of IgM to IgG ratios reinforced the picture of an IgG-dominated early response to SARS-CoV-2. Infected individuals showed significantly lower IgM:IgG ratios against SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid and spike than controls, as early as 0 to 7 days after infection, and no significant shift in the ratios occurred between the two time windows. For the seasonal coronaviruses, anti-spike IgM:IgG ratios showed no significant differences between infected individuals and controls, remaining uniformly low for HCoV-229E, HCoV-HKU1 and HCoV-OC43. The exception was HCoV-NL63, where the IgM:IgG ratio was elevated in infected individuals, reaching statistical significance at 8 to 14 days, mirroring the elevated IgM levels against that virus. The study also documented baseline cross-reactivity in the pre-pandemic controls. No pre-pandemic seropositivity was observed for SARS-CoV-2 spike for any isotype, but the controls did show seropositivity for the receptor binding domain, at 17 percent for IgG, 10 percent for IgA and 13 percent for IgM, and low-level seropositivity for nucleocapsid in 3 percent for IgA and IgG. The authors note that the receptor binding domain is a smaller protein that yields lower signals and lower positivity thresholds, increasing the likelihood of false positives, and that pre-pandemic cross-reactivity rates can vary with age, year and region. The authors are careful about what the findings do and do not show. The cohort consisted of unvaccinated individuals infected with ancestral SARS-CoV-2, which the authors describe as a valuable reference point for defining early antibody kinetics without confounding from vaccination or reinfection, but the sample was small, drawn largely from hospitalized cases, and lacked clinical data on severity, comorbidities and sex-stratified analyses. There were no paired specimens for individual-level longitudinal follow-up, and the assay measured antibody quantities rather than function, so the cross-reactivity cannot be tied to neutralization or protection. The authors also cannot determine whether the early seasonal coronavirus responses reflect true antibody cross-reactivity or recall of conserved epitopes from prior exposures. Even so, they conclude that the early IgG, IgA and IgM responses to SARS-CoV-2 were associated with seasonal coronavirus responses, supporting earlier pandemic reports that IgM-based tests for recent infection are unreliable for SARS-CoV-2, and underscoring the importance of accounting for cross-reactivity when interpreting serological assays and assessing correlates of protection. Subject of Research: Cross-reactive antibody responses to seasonal human coronaviruses following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection Article Title: Cross-reactive IgM, IgA, and IgG antibody responses to seasonal human coronaviruses following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection Article References: Tanunliong, G., Márquez, A. C., Krajden, M., Morshed, M., Jassem, A. N., & Sekirov, I. (2026). Cross-reactive IgM, IgA, and IgG antibody responses to seasonal human coronaviruses following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection. Discover Viruses, 3(1), Article 1. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44370-026-00036-1 Image Credits: AI Generated DOI: 10.1007/s44370-026-00036-1 Keywords: SARS-CoV-2, human coronaviruses, cross-reactivity, IgM, IgG, IgA, serology, antibody kinetics, HCoV-OC43, HCoV-HKU1, multiplex immunoassay, immune imprinting News Source: Kristina Jarvis. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Hydrophobic loop remodeling weakens ACE2 binding in SARS-CoV-2 JN.4 by October 27, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Hydrophobic loop remodeling weakens ACE2 binding in SARS-CoV-2 JN.4 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram The SARS-CoV-2 Omicron subvariant JN.4 carries a unique A475V substitution in the receptor binding domain (RBD), yet has shown limited expansion compared with its parallel descendant JN.1. A new study investigates how hydrophobic remodeling within the RBD large loop, spanning residues 475 to 490, modulates receptor engagement and spike function, offering a structural explanation for the variant’s constrained fitness. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the researchers found that A475V induces local remodeling of the receptor-binding motif and alters the geometry of the RBD–ACE2 interaction. Local refinement showed that the bulky valine substitution disrupts the interaction network surrounding residue 475, producing a 3.5-fold reduction in ACE2-binding affinity relative to BA.2.86. Unlike the L455S substitution in JN.1, which primarily alters the receptor-binding interface, A475V within the flexible large loop influences both local loop conformation and global spike conformational properties. Systematic mutagenesis identified A475 and F486 as functionally constrained hydrophobic residues that preserve the structural framework of ACE2 engagement despite extensive sequence variation in the surrounding loop. Molecular dynamics simulations and functional assays supported these structural observations, indicating that the loop tolerates sequence change only within limits set by receptor recognition and conformational stability. Discover more Read Med Journals Study Biology Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Study Chemistry The findings establish the RBD 475–490 large loop as a structurally plastic yet functionally constrained element that balances receptor recognition, conformational stability, and antigenic diversification. The authors present this as a mechanistic framework for understanding region-specific evolutionary constraints that shape SARS-CoV-2 RBD adaptation. Because the work combines structural biology, simulation, and functional testing, it links a single amino acid change to measurable effects on receptor binding and spike behavior, clarifying why JN.4 has not followed the same expansion trajectory as JN.1 despite sharing recent ancestry within the Omicron radiation. Balogun the latest to be linked 8hESPN What soccer stars did for Halloween: James the Joker, DracuLucas, more 13hChris Wright Pulisic staying in Milan reflects his club career: Good, but not quite great 2dJeff Carlisle Man United implode at Chelsea, and, make no mistake, they are in a Premier League relegation battle 1dMark Ogden Are Man City fans right about a Premier League 'Red Cartel' that's out to get them? 2dMark Ogden Ronaldo goal review: Why his 982nd career strike should be an own goal instead 2dAndy Davies Global power ranking: The top 20 soccer teams in the world, ranked! 2dRyan O'Hanlon Man City, Bayern among the good, bad and lucky in Europe's top leagues 3dBill Connelly Xhaka, Embolo to return for Switzerland after fake COVID-19 documents case play Breel Embolo gets on the scoresheet for Atlanta United FC (1:02) ESPN News Services Multiple Authors Oct 27, 2026, 12:16 PM ET Share Copy Link Email Print Granit Xhaka was restored as captain of Switzerland on Tuesday after missing four games because he admitted using fake vaccination certificates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Atlanta United forward Breel Embolo, who was further implicated in September in a similar case, also can be picked again for two Nations League matches next month, the Swiss soccer federation said in a statement. "I am pleased once again to be able to make my selections without restrictions for the November games," Switzerland coach Murat Yakin said. Yakin, his staff and players were unanimous in wanting Xhaka to continue as captain, the federation said. Xhaka revealed this month he was put on two years' probation for getting a fake vaccine document in 2022. He paid court costs with a suspended fine of 150,000 Swiss francs ($180,000). The Sunderland captain can add to his national-team record of 152 caps when Switzerland play in Slovenia on Nov. 13 and host Scotland three days later. Embolo, who joined MLS side Atlanta United in August, has 26 goals in 92 appearances for the Swiss. World Cup quarterfinalists Switzerland top their Nations League second-tier group, five points ahead of Slovenia, seeking promotion back to the top tier. Services will restart on Thursday, September 9. The Iloilo provincial capitol announced on Tuesday, September 7, a temporary shutdown of services after 15 personnel tested positive for COVID-19. Provincial Administrator Suzette Mamon said the move would allow “maximum contact tracing and disinfection.” Services will restart on Thursday, September 9. On the other side of Western Visayas, Negros Occidental provincial officials were eyeing levels of lockdown of two hospitals after a doctor and a nurse tested positive for COVID-19. A doctor from the Teresita Jalandoni Provincial Hospital in Silay City was taken from an isolation center to the Corazon Locsin Montelibano Memorial Hospital because of worsening symptoms, the province’s COVID-19 task force announced. A nurse from a different hospital was already recovering. The Don Jose S. Monfort Medical Center Extension Hospital in Barotac Nuevo, Iloilo, also temporarily suspended elective surgeries until September 13 to conduct contact tracing and disinfection. It did not give any figures for infected staff. In Iloilo City, Mayor Jerry Treñas said three priests, a cook, and a secretary of a church in La Paz district had also tested positive for the virus. The mayor did not give details but Aksyon Radyo Iloilo said 31 personnel of the church are under quarantine. Treñas on Tuesday added seven more barangays to the local granular lockdown list, bringing to 36 the number of areas where egress and ingress – except by health officials – will be banned for 72 hours. Areas are placed under granular lockdown if there are two or more COVID-19 cases. The mayor assured communities that affected households would receive food and other aid. The lockdown involves mandatory reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) tests of close contacts and contact tracing for second tier contacts. Iloilo City recorded 159 new COVID-19 cases on Monday, September 6, and 105 the day before. “Our cases keep rising so please stay at home and get yourselves vaccinated,” the mayor urged. Must Read Slow delivery of vaccines blamed for COVID-19 deaths in Bacolod, Iloilo COVID-19 cases also kept rising in Negros Occigental, where Governor Eugenio Jose “Bon” Lacson said active cases have once more surged past the 1,000 mark. Bacolod City, meanwhile, reported two new Delta cases, including a hospital healthcare worker, tracing 11 close contacts and putting them on lockdown until their test results come out. Lacson said the most affected cities in the province are Bago, just south of Bacolod, E.B. Magalona in the province’s middle northern part, and San Carlos City in the far north. Local executives also had good news for constituents. Treñas announced free RT-PCR tests at the city’s Jubilee Hall for all symptomatic patients and their contacts, returning overseas Filipinos, and returning residents. He also asked the city council to put a P1,800 cap on the price of RT-PCR tests to help businesses that need to continuously test employees. The mayor said residents need a doctor’s referral to get free tests. “Those who will undergo a swab test for travel or employment purposes will be charged with the current rate of P2,500 pending the amendment in the ordinance,” Treñas said. The Philippine Red Cross also announced a price drop for RT-PCR tests. It slashed the price of its swab test by a thousand pesos, from P3,800 to P2,800. The price for the saliva-based test is now P1,500, from P2,000. Bacolod City Administrator Em Ang reported the launch of the city’s fourth vaccination bus and a return to workplace inoculation, saying it would help speed up goals to achieve herd immunity. – Rappler.com Add to Preferred Sources Share in Chat Share article Facebook X (Twitter) Copy Link Copied How does this make you feel? content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Teenager with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS recovers after a year of multifaceted care, case report says by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Teenager with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS recovers after a year of multifaceted care, case report says Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A 17-year-old high-school student who became bedridden for more than half of each day after a SARS-CoV-2 infection has made a full recovery from post-COVID-19 myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, according to a case report published in BioPsychoSocial Medicine on 10 September 2026. The report, authored by Takakazu Oka, describes how the patient, who had already received treatments at other medical facilities without returning to school, was ultimately able to enter university approximately one year after her initial consultation. Post-COVID-19 ME/CFS is a condition in which some people infected with SARS-CoV-2 develop persistent fatigue and cognitive dysfunction that meet the diagnostic criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome. The report notes that no established treatment exists for this condition, and that accounts of patients who have recovered remain limited. Because the pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying the disabling symptoms are not yet fully understood, the author adopted a multifaceted treatment approach that considered disease severity, functional level, illness beliefs and coping behaviors, social support systems, comorbidities, secondary issues, and the phase of recovery. The treatment programme described in the case presentation comprised ten components introduced progressively and tailored to the patient’s phase of recovery. These were instruction on eating habits and supplements; instruction on physical activities; instruction on managing cognitive fatigue; environmental adjustment; pharmacotherapy with midodrine, ibudilast, and the traditional Japanese herbal medicines hochuekkito and tokishakuyakusan; facilitation of therapeutic interoceptive awareness; adjustment of disrupted diurnal sleep-wake rhythms; conditioning exercise; instructions for safe recovery; and nurturing self-efficacy. Discover more Find Treatments Get Health Tips Book Care Services Get Rapid Tests According to the report, the patient was referred to the author’s department for severe fatigue that developed after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Despite treatments at other facilities, she remained bedridden for more than half of each day and was unable to attend school. After the progressive, multiperspective interventions, the report states that approximately one year after her initial consultation she made a full recovery, entered university, and is now enjoying university life. The author concludes that the report describes, in detail, the evaluation and multifaceted treatment of a 17-year-old high-school student with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS who had been unable to attend school but who ultimately recovered and was able to attend university. As a single-patient case report, the findings describe one individual’s course of care and cannot by themselves establish the efficacy of any component of the treatment approach for post-COVID-19 ME/CFS more broadly, a limitation consistent with the report’s own observation that no established treatment exists and that recovery reports remain limited. The article was published as an open-access case report and, at the time of this writing, was shared as an early, peer-reviewed accepted version subject to further edits before the final version of record.
