Image Courtesy: Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar HEALTHCARE Create Bookmark RSV poses greater risk of hospitalization for children than flu or COVID-19, Qatar study finds The findings underscore the importance of strengthening preventive strategies Press Release Doha – Researchers at Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar (WCM-Q) and Sidra Medicine, in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health and Hamad Medical Corporation, have found that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) was associated with substantially more severe illness than influenza or COVID-19 among children in Qatar. The findings underscore the importance of strengthening preventive strategies, including increasing vaccination uptake and expanding access to long-acting monoclonal antibodies against RSV, to reduce the burden of severe respiratory illness among children. Published in the prestigious journal The Lancet Regional Health – Eastern Mediterranean, the study analyzed a large, systematically collected dataset comprising 4,360 respiratory illness episodes among 3,932 children younger than 18 years who attended Sidra Medicine’s emergency department between January 2022 and December 2025. Sidra Medicine serves as Qatar’s national referral center for specialized pediatric care. The study encompassed the entire pediatric age spectrum, from infancy through adolescence, and assessed disease severity based on hospitalization and intensive care unit admission. The study is the first from the Eastern Mediterranean Region to directly compare the severity of RSV, influenza, and COVID-19 across the full pediatric age spectrum, from infancy through adolescence. By examining all three viruses over four years of concurrent circulation within a single national pediatric referral setting, the study addresses important limitations of previous research worldwide, which has often been restricted to comparisons between two viruses, specific age groups, or different periods of viral circulation. These findings make an important contribution to the international evidence base while providing much-needed regional evidence to inform clinical care, public health strategies, and immunization policies. The study found that RSV was associated with substantially more severe illness than either influenza or COVID-19, while the latter two infections showed broadly similar severity. Influenza accounted for 65% of the illness episodes studied, followed by COVID-19 at 22% and RSV at just 13%. Despite its smaller share of illnesses, hospital admission was approximately four times as common with RSV as with either of the other infections, and intensive care admission was more than three times as common. This pattern remained after accounting for differences in patient characteristics and was consistent across age groups, although RSV predominantly affected younger children. Dr. Andres Perez-Lopez, Chief of the Microbiology Division at Sidra Medicine, who co-led the study and oversaw its microbiological and clinical components, said: “One of the most striking findings was how strongly a child’s underlying health influenced the severity of respiratory infections. Children with pre-existing medical conditions had nearly seven times greater chances of hospitalization and twelve times greater chances of requiring intensive care compared with children without these conditions. These findings highlight the importance of identifying vulnerable children early and ensuring they receive appropriate monitoring, preventive care, and medical care.” Dr. Hiam Chemaitelly, Assistant Professor of Research in Population Health Sciences at WCM-Q, who designed and co-led the study and oversaw its epidemiological component, said: “It was striking to see how frequently RSV led to hospitalization and how much could be gained through prevention. Fortunately, effective interventions are now available, including RSV vaccination during pregnancy to protect newborns and long-acting monoclonal antibodies that protect infants during their most vulnerable early months. Increasing uptake of these interventions, supported by conversations with families during routine pregnancy care, could help prevent severe illness and avoidable hospitalizations. Equally important is improving influenza and COVID-19 vaccination uptake among children, as these infections can also cause serious illness. Raising awareness among families and encouraging the use of these preventive measures are essential to protecting children’s health.” The study, titled “Relative severity of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus among pediatric emergency department attendees in Qatar: a retrospective cohort study,” was supported by the Qatar Research, Development and Innovation Council through grant ARG02-0402-240119. Collaborators included Qatar’s Ministry of Public Health, and Hamad Medical Corporation. About Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar is a partnership between Cornell University and Qatar Foundation. It offers a comprehensive Six-Year Medical Program leading to the Cornell University M.D. degree with teaching by Cornell and Weill Cornell faculty and by physicians at Hamad Medical Corporation (HMC), Sidra Medicine, the Primary Health Care Corporation, and Aspetar Orthopedic and Sports Medicine Hospital, who hold Weill Cornell appointments. Through its biomedical research program, WCM-Q is building a sustainable research community in Qatar while advancing basic science and clinical research. Through its medical college, WCM-Q seeks to provide the finest education possible for medical students, to improve health care both now and for future generations, and to provide high quality health care to the Qatari population. These findings highlight the importance of identifying vulnerable children early and ensuring they receive appropriate monitoring, preventive care, and medical care.” Dr. Hiam Chemaitelly, assistant professor of Research in Population Health Sciences at WCM-Q, who designed and co-led the study and oversaw its epidemiological component, said: “It was striking to see how frequently RSV led to hospitalisation and how much could be gained through prevention. Fortunately, effective interventions are now available, including RSV vaccination during pregnancy to protect newborns and long-acting monoclonal antibodies that protect infants during their most vulnerable early months. Increasing uptake of these interventions, supported by conversations with families during routine pregnancy care, could help prevent severe illness and avoidable hospitalisations. Equally important is improving influenza and COVID-19 vaccination uptake among children, as these infections can also cause serious illness.” The study, titled “Relative severity of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus among paediatric emergency department attendees in Qatar: a retrospective cohort study,” was supported by the Qatar Research, Development and Innovation Council through grant ARG02-0402-240119. Collaborators included Qatar’s Ministry of Public Health, and Hamad Medical Corporation. Copy 29/10/2026 40

Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月31日 来源:Health Science Reports 2.9 编辑推荐: 背景与目的 COVID-19可导致感染后持续存在的症状,即所谓的长新冠(Long COVID)。本研究旨在明确经确诊的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2型(SARS-CoV-2)感染者以及医护人员中持续性体征和症状的患病率。 方法 本研究为系统综述与Meta分析,遵 免费下载【类器官培养与鉴定指南】,帮您快速选择不同类器官培养所需的细胞因子和标志物抗体。 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW Open Access 背景与目的 COVID-19可导致感染后持续存在的症状,即所谓的长新冠(Long COVID)。本研究旨在明确经确诊的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2型(SARS-CoV-2)感染者以及医护人员中持续性体征和症状的患病率。 方法 本研究为系统综述与Meta分析,遵循系统综述和Meta分析首选报告条目(PRISMA)指南,并已在国际前瞻性系统综述注册库(PROSPERO)注册(注册号:CRD42023460632)。纳入标准为COVID-19感染后随访时间至少12周的队列研究。检索于2023年11月在PubMed、Scopus、Embase、Scielo及LILACS/BVS数据库以及灰色文献中进行。采用Rayyan软件进行文献筛选,并在R软件中对各症状进行合并患病率Meta分析。方法学质量采用纽卡斯尔-渥太华量表(NOS)进行评估。 结果 共检索到2,456项研究,其中59篇文献纳入系统综述,58篇纳入Meta分析,涉及196,863名参与者。合并患病率(95%置信区间[CI])最高的症状为疲劳(0.29[0.24–0.36],95%预测区间[PI]:0.05–0.78)和呼吸困难(0.16[0.12–0.22],95% PI:0.01–0.71)。 结论 医护人员在部分持续性症状(疲劳、呼吸困难、咳嗽、味觉改变及胃肠道症状)上的患病率低于普通人群。多数研究质量为中等。尽管研究发现持续性症状的患病率较高,但高异质性仍是主要局限性。 论文主体内容总结 索取CAR-T 细胞免疫疗法最新资料领 取 1 引言 COVID-19由SARS-CoV-2病毒引起,全球已导致超过7.75亿例感染和700余万例死亡。急性期主要累及呼吸系统,表现为咳嗽、呼吸困难、流涕和咽痛等症状,亦可出现胃肠道、肌肉骨骼、神经、发热、嗅觉与味觉功能障碍及心脏表现。疾病严重程度差异显著,部分患者症状轻微,部分则需住院治疗及出院后随访。疫情进展中逐渐认识到该病可导致长期系统性受累,即持续性症状与后遗症,被称为新冠后综合征或长新冠。英国国家健康与临床优化研究所(NICE)与世界卫生组织(WHO)将其定义为感染急性期后症状持续超过3个月(12周)且无法以其他诊断解释的状况。最常见的持续性症状包括疲劳、呼吸困难、肌痛、头痛、嗅觉与味觉丧失及运动不耐受。医护人员长期处于抗疫一线,面临工作流程改变和照护后勤调整,加之个人防护装备(PPE)短缺,感染风险升高。据此提出研究问题:普通人群和医护人员中SARS-CoV-2感染所致的持续性体征和症状中哪些最为普遍?本研究旨在明确感染普通人群及医护人员中COVID-19持续性体征和症状的患病率。 2 材料与方法 2.1 设计 本研究为系统文献综述与Meta分析,遵循PRISMA原则,并于2023年9月5日在PROSPERO注册(编号CRD42023460632)。该方案亦支持已发表的关于COVID-19心理与认知后遗症的系统综述,两项综述目标与结局不同,检索策略和纳入标准共享,但数据提取和Meta分析分别独立进行。 2.2 检索方法 于2023年11月在PubMed、Scopus、Embase、Scielo和LILACS/BVS数据库中进行检索,并辅以纳入研究参考文献列表的手工检索和灰色文献检索。采用健康科学描述符(DeCS)和医学主题词表(MeSH)中的“Post-Acute COVID-19 Syndrome”“Long COVID”“Cohort Studies”等术语,结合布尔运算符OR和AND构建各数据库检索策略。采用PECOs策略:人群(P)为普通人群和医护人员;暴露(E)为SARS-CoV-2感染;无对照组(C);结局(O)为持续性COVID-19体征和症状;研究类型(s)为观察性队列研究。 2.3 纳入与排除标准 纳入经聚合酶链反应(PCR)或抗原检测确诊SARS-CoV-2感染、且依据WHO和NICE定义评估感染后持续性症状的纵向观察性队列研究。排除仅凭临床评估或疑似病例诊断的研究、基于血清学诊断且无法估计感染后随访时间的研究、纯儿科人群、感染后随访不足3个月或随访时间不明的研究,以及数据不足且作者在两次联系后1个月内未回复的研究。 2.4 数据处理 检索结果导入Endnote去除重复文献,其余文献上传至Rayyan,由两名独立评审者进行筛选,分歧经协商解决,无法达成一致时由第三名专家裁定。评审者间一致性采用kappa统计量评估。筛选完成后将数据导出至作者设计的Excel表格,提取研究标识、样本特征及COVID-19诊断后随访时长等变量。当随访时间以范围报告时,取中点值归入分析组,可能导致随访时长分类偏差。 2.5 检索结局 研究结局为持续性COVID-19体征和症状,初始逐项提取且不进行数据填补,信息缺失时联系作者。为便于Meta分析,临床相关结局归入预定义症状类别(疲劳:疲劳、疲倦、虚弱、体能下降和运动不耐受;心悸:心悸和心动过速)。同一类别内报告多个结局时仅纳入单一估计值以避免重复计数,并选取患病率最高者。 2.6 数据提取 Meta分析在R软件4.4.1版本中使用“meta”包7.0-0版本进行,采用随机效应模型和逆方差法。合并前进行logit转换,研究间方差(τ2)采用限制性最大似然(REML)法估计。各持续性症状分别以95%置信区间进行患病率Meta分析。异质性采用Q检验和I2不一致指数计算,显著性水平设为p≤0.05。I2≤25%视为同质,>25%且<75%为中度异质性,≥75%为高度异质性。鉴于所有结局均呈现高异质性,依据参与者是否为医护人员、感染后随访时间、队列类型、研究地点、住院状态和研究质量进行亚组分析。未进行敏感性分析,理由是纳入研究存在临床和方法学异质性,剔除单项研究不太可能实质性改变总体结果。 2.7 质量评价 采用适用于队列研究的纽卡斯尔-渥太华量表(NOS)评估方法学质量,该量表涵盖参与者选择、组间可比性及结局和随访评估三个领域。依据总分将研究分为差(0–3星)、中等(4–6星)和良好(7–9星)。采用Egger检验和漏斗图评估各结局的发表偏倚。未进行证据确定性评估,因纳入研究均为疫情背景下的队列研究,假定存在较高偏倚风险。 3 结果 文献检索共获得2,456篇相关文章,去除1,229篇重复文献后,经标题和摘要筛选,203篇进行全文评估,其中141篇因不符合纳入/排除标准或数据提取不足被排除,4篇因属同一队列被排除,1篇无法获取全文,灰色文献中纳入1篇。最终59篇纳入系统综述,其中58篇进入定量分析,1篇因仅报告单一未纳入定量分析的结局而被排除。系统综述总人群为196,863名参与者。kappa指数为κ=0.792(p<0.001),表明一致性较好。58篇Meta分析文献中,6篇专门针对医护人员,2篇同时包含医护人员和普通人群并进行分层分析,故共8项研究涉及医护人员。多数研究为前瞻性队列(81.4%),质量以中等为主(89.8%)。样本量从27人到127,859人不等。普通人群平均年龄为31.3至71岁,医护人员为34.4至42.2岁。随访期从感染确诊后3至24个月不等。地理分布上,多数研究来自欧洲(32项),其次为南美洲和北美洲(各9项)、亚洲(7项)、非洲(1项),另有1项跨欧洲和南美洲的多国研究。Meta分析合并患病率(95%CI)最高的结局依次为:疲劳(0.29[0.24;0.36],95% PI:0.05–0.78,I2=98.9%)、呼吸困难(0.16[0.12;0.22],95% PI:0.01–0.71,I2=99.5%)、关节痛(0.12[0.07;0.19],95% PI:0.01–0.72,I2=97.8%)、肌痛(0.11[0.07;0.16],95% PI:0.01–0.59,I2=98.4%)、头痛(0.10[0.07;0.13],95% PI:0.01–0.53,I2=99.5%)、脱发(0.09[0.06;0.13],95% PI:0.01–0.42,I2=98.7%)、嗅觉功能障碍(0.08[0.06;0.12],95% PI:0.01–0.45,I2=97.2%)和心悸(0.08[0.05;0.12],95% PI:0.01–0.49,I2=98.4%)。患病率较低的结局包括咳嗽、头晕/昏厥、胸痛/胸闷、味觉改变、胃肠道症状、皮肤改变和发热/寒战。亚组分析显示,医护人员在疲劳、呼吸困难、咳嗽、味觉改变和胃肠道症状上的合并患病率显著低于普通人群(p<0.05),其中味觉改变和胃肠道症状在医护人员中的异质性显著降低(I2<25%)。随访时间未显示症状患病率的显著差异。地理因素对多数结局有显著影响,但可能受欧洲、南美和北美研究集中的影响。前瞻性研究在疲劳、头痛、心悸、咳嗽和胃肠道症状上的患病率高于回顾性研究。住院状态与呼吸困难、咳嗽、心悸和头晕/昏厥四种症状的差异显著相关,咳嗽在住院患者中更为普遍。 4 讨论 本系统综述结果表明,确诊SARS-CoV-2感染的个体在急性疾病消退后仍经历持续性症状,可能影响其生活质量、日常活动、返岗复工,并给医疗系统带来额外负担。预测区间较宽与研究间高异质性一致,结果应谨慎解读。异质性可能反映研究人群、住院状态、随访时长、流行病毒变异株、疫苗接种状态、症状确定方法和地理差异等方面的不同。疲劳是最普遍的症状(合并患病率为0.29),可能与免疫失调和细胞能量代谢改变有关,包括线粒体功能受损。持续性呼吸困难和咳嗽是临床关注重点,可能源于病毒所致的残余肺损伤或炎症。肌肉骨骼症状如肌痛和关节痛可能反映持续的炎症状态。嗅觉和味觉功能障碍在急性期常见,其持续存在与认知损害相关。皮肤问题如皮疹和脱发亦较常见,尤其在女性中。头痛为第五常见症状,可见于有无头痛病史的个体。心血管症状如胸痛和心悸在感染期间和感染后均有报道。胃肠道症状和发热/寒战患病率较低,可能并非新冠后综合征的核心特征。亚组分析中,医护人员在疲劳、呼吸困难、咳嗽、味觉改变和胃肠道症状上的患病率显著较低,可能反映其优先获得疫苗接种、平均年龄较年轻、症状报告不足或早期识别和治疗等因素,但这些解释应视为假设而非因果推断。漏斗图不对称性提示疲劳、肌痛、脱发和发热/寒战的合并患病率估计可能受报告偏倚影响,应谨慎解读。 5 优势与局限性 本研究的优势在于同时分析多个结局(15种症状),可识别患病率最高者,且样本广泛且稳健。主要局限性包括依赖自我报告症状,可能受主观感知影响导致低估或高估;许多研究纳入住院或门诊患者,急性期症状较重者可能具有更高的感染后症状患病率,无症状或轻症个体可能代表性不足;疫情背景下研究的方法学和人群差异可能导致高异质性;部分结局存在小研究效应,提示可能存在发表偏倚。 打赏 展开全文 content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Folic acid food fortification linked to lower COVID-19 incidence in country-level analysis by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Folic acid food fortification linked to lower COVID-19 incidence in country-level analysis Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Countries that mandate folic acid fortification of foods reported substantially lower COVID-19 incidence than countries without such policies, according to a peer-reviewed study published in BMC Public Health. In analyses stratified by World Health Organization region, mandatory fortification in Africa and Europe was associated with roughly 70 percent lower COVID-19 incidence, while no statistically significant association emerged for mortality. The research team, led by Wendy N. Nembhard and colleagues, set out to test a hypothesis that circulated widely during the pandemic: that SARS-CoV-2 might co-opt folate metabolism to support viral replication. Some earlier studies had suggested that folic acid supplementation could decrease the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection while potentially increasing the risk of death after infection, prompting the authors to examine whether population-level folic acid intake through food fortification was associated with COVID-19 outcomes at the country level. To conduct the analysis, the team drew country-specific data on folic acid fortification policy status, the extent of grain fortification, and total adjusted potential folic acid food intake from the Global Fortification Data Exchange. COVID-19 incidence and mortality data covering December 2019 through April 2023 came from the World Health Organization. Countries were grouped into WHO regions and World Bank income classes to account for the enormous differences in health systems, demographics, and pandemic trajectories across the globe. The statistical approach centered on negative binomial regression, a model suited to count data such as infection and death counts, which the researchers used to estimate rate ratios and 95 percent confidence intervals for COVID-19 incidence and mortality per 100,000 population. These estimates were stratified by region and income group, allowing the authors to compare fortification status within, rather than across, broadly similar groupings of countries. Discover more food fortification Explore Food Tech Order Vitamins COVID-19 Get Rapid Tests Because countries that fortify foods differ systematically from those that do not, in wealth, age structure, population size, and geography, the researchers also performed propensity score analyses. These models adjusted for gender and age distribution, population size, country-level income, and geographical region, attempting to mimic the balance of a controlled experiment by comparing fortification and non-fortification countries that were otherwise similar on measured characteristics. The headline result held in both Africa and Europe: countries with mandatory folic acid fortification policies had approximately 70 percent lower COVID-19 incidence than countries without such policies, with a rate ratio of 0.26 in Africa (95 percent confidence interval 0.11 to 0.60) and 0.27 in Europe (95 percent confidence interval 0.13 to 0.57). When the propensity score models pooled countries across regions and adjusted for income and other covariates, the difference in COVID-19 incidence between fortification and non-fortification countries remained statistically significant. Mortality told a different story. Across the analyses, including the propensity score models, the researchers found no statistically significant association between folic acid fortification and COVID-19 mortality. The authors concluded that folic acid fortification was associated with lower COVID-19 incidence after adjusting for income and region, but not with mortality, and they emphasized that additional studies are needed to investigate the association further. The study's design carries important limitations that the authors and readers must weigh. This is an ecological, country-level comparison rather than a study of individuals, so it cannot establish that folic acid intake caused any person's infection risk to fall. Unmeasured differences between countries, from testing capacity and reporting practices to pandemic timing and public health measures, could contribute to the observed patterns, and the fortification exposure reflects potential intake at the population level rather than measured individual consumption. The findings therefore stand as an observational signal, one that the researchers say warrants further investigation rather than a demonstration of protective effect. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Gum Disease Inflammation Activates Viral Entry Pathways Tied to SARS-CoV-2 by October 27, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Gum Disease Inflammation Activates Viral Entry Pathways Tied to SARS-CoV-2 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram SARS-CoV-2 is best known as a respiratory pathogen, but the oral cavity has increasingly drawn attention as a site where viral activity, receptor expression, microbial communities, and inflammation intersect. A new study published open access in BMC Infectious Diseases on 26 October 2026 reports that periodontal disease, a chronic dysbiotic inflammatory condition of the tissues supporting the teeth, is associated with heightened activity of a non-canonical viral entry pathway that SARS-CoV-2 can potentially exploit. The research, led by Afsar Naqvi and colleagues, focused on the phosphatidylserine, or PS, dependent entry route, which involves the TIM family of receptors and related enzymes, and asked whether the inflamed gum environment characteristic of periodontitis primes this pathway. The team examined expression of genes belonging to the PS-dependent pathway, including ADAM17, ATP11c, TIM1, TIM3, and TIM4, across three settings: gingival tissue, saliva, and human oral keratinocytes grown in the laboratory. In prepandemic gum biopsy samples, inflamed periodontal tissue showed significant upregulation of all of these non-canonical receptors compared with healthy tissue. According to the authors, this indicates that periodontal disease on its own establishes a molecular environment associated with PS-mediated microbial entry markers, independent of any exposure to SARS-CoV-2. The researchers then turned to a post-vaccination cohort to look for the same molecular patterns in a clinical context. Salivary expression of the PS-dependent pathway genes was markedly elevated in individuals who tested positive for COVID-19 and also had periodontal disease. These same individuals showed significantly increased levels of phosphatidylserine in their saliva. The authors interpret this as a co-occurring pattern of viral exposure and periodontal inflammation rather than proof that gum disease causes infection, and they frame the relationship as an association between COVID-19 and periodontal disease with implications for viral activity, immune dysregulation, and long-term oral health. To probe the mechanism more directly, the group performed in vitro experiments using primary human oral keratinocytes, the epithelial cells that line the mouth. When these cells were exposed to SARS-CoV-2 together with periodontal pathogens, specifically Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, the combination induced robust and concordant activation of PS-dependent entry genes, with the TIM family receptors showing particularly strong responses. This laboratory finding suggests that the co-presence of the virus and periodontal bacteria can drive the same molecular program observed in patient tissues, although results from cultured cells do not by themselves demonstrate that this occurs in the human body or that it increases actual viral infectivity. The study's design carries important limitations that shape how the findings should be read. The human data are observational: the prepandemic biopsies establish that inflamed gum tissue expresses more PS-pathway genes, and the cohort data show that COVID-19-positive individuals with periodontal disease carry higher salivary levels of those genes and of phosphatidylserine, but neither result establishes a causal chain from gum inflammation to viral entry. The in vitro work demonstrates pathway activation under controlled co-exposure conditions rather than measured enhancement of SARS-CoV-2 infection. The published version is also an early-share, peer-reviewed accepted manuscript that remains subject to further edits before the final version of record appears. Even with those caveats, the work adds a specific molecular dimension to evidence linking oral health and COVID-19. Rather than invoking general inflammation alone, the study identifies a defined receptor system, the PS/TIM axis, whose components are measurably elevated in diseased gum tissue, in the saliva of co-affected patients, and in oral epithelial cells challenged with both the virus and periodontal bacteria. The authors suggest that this inflammatory environment co-occurs with molecular conditions related to SARS-CoV-2 infection pathways in the oral mucosa, positioning periodontal status as a potential modifier of susceptibility at the viral entry surface itself. A., Elshourbagy, S., Etminan, S., Sandoval, G., Bambrilla, M., Nares, S., Schwartz, J., Shukla, D., Class, J., Richner, J., & Naqvi, A. (2026). content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Chemistry Compound from Algerian Desert Plant Shows Antifungal Activity and SARS-CoV-2 Binding in Lab Tests by October 29, 2026 in Chemistry Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Compound from Algerian Desert Plant Shows Antifungal Activity and SARS-CoV-2 Binding in Lab Tests Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Chemists have isolated a pentacyclic triterpenoid compound from the aerial parts of Launaea arborescens, a shrub widely distributed in southwestern Algeria, and report that it inhibits the growth of several Candida fungal species in laboratory assays while also showing favorable computed binding to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease. The compound, abbreviated HIHPT for heptamethyl–icosahydropicene–triol, was identified as 4,4,6b,8a,11,11,14b-heptamethyl-1,2,3,4,4a,5,6,6a,6b,7,8,8a,9,10,11,12,12a,14,14a,14b-icosahydropicene-3,5,8-triol, a molecule carrying three hydroxyl groups on a five-ring carbon skeleton. The extraction began with powdered, dehydrated aerial parts of the plant processed through a Soxhlet apparatus using solvents of increasing polarity: diethyl ether, dichloromethane, ethyl acetate, and n-butanol. The dichloromethane extract showed the highest biological activity among the crude fractions and was therefore selected for purification. Silica gel column chromatography with chloroform/petroleum ether and chloroform/methanol gradient elution yielded five fractions, and the bioactive compound was isolated from the fifth fraction as a white powder melting at 62 to 63 degrees Celsius. Spectroscopic characterization by infrared, proton and carbon nuclear magnetic resonance, and mass spectrometry established the molecular formula C29H48O3, with elemental analysis closely matching the calculated carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen percentages. The antifungal evaluation used five clinical fungal isolates obtained from the Microbiology Laboratory of the University Hospital of Annaba, Algeria: Candida albicans, Candida krusei, Candida kefyr, Candida lusitaniae, and Candida tropicalis. Susceptibility was determined by the agar well diffusion method following Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidelines. A stock solution of 5 milligrams of HIHPT per milliliter of dimethyl sulfoxide was prepared freshly under sterile conditions, and 20 microliters were dispensed into 6-millimeter wells punched into Sabouraud Dextrose Agar plates seeded with fungal suspensions adjusted to 0.5 McFarland turbidity. Amphotericin B served as the positive control, while the solvent and sterile distilled water served as negative controls. Plates were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 24 hours, and inhibition zones were measured in millimeters. Discover more Save on Rx Compare Lab Gear Study Chemistry Identify Plants Check Symptoms The results showed activity against four of the five tested species. The strongest effect appeared against Candida krusei, with a 35-millimeter inhibition zone compared with 20 millimeters for amphotericin B, a notable result because C. krusei is recognized for its intrinsic resistance to several conventional antifungal agents. Against Candida albicans, HIHPT produced a 28-millimeter zone while amphotericin B was recorded as resistant, meaning no measurable inhibition under the assay conditions. Candida lusitaniae showed a 22-millimeter zone with HIHPT, again with the reference drug recorded as resistant, and Candida tropicalis displayed a 16-millimeter zone for HIHPT versus 8 millimeters for amphotericin B. No activity was observed against Candida kefyr, and the DMSO negative control produced no inhibition for any strain, indicating the observed effects were attributable to the compound itself. Beyond planktonic growth, the team assessed biofilm formation using a crystal violet staining assay in 96-well polystyrene plates, measuring optical density at 620 nanometers after 24 hours of incubation. HIHPT inhibited biofilm formation across all five Candida isolates, with the highest inhibition against Candida albicans at 46.54 percent, followed by Candida kefyr at 36.46 percent, Candida lusitaniae at 33.87 percent, Candida krusei at 30.90 percent, and Candida tropicalis at 22.77 percent. Amphotericin B, by contrast, showed only weak biofilm inhibition against C. krusei and C. tropicalis and little or no inhibition against the remaining species under the same conditions. Because biofilm formation is a major virulence factor contributing to antifungal resistance and recurrent candidiasis, compounds that suppress it are considered promising leads, although the authors note that minimum inhibitory concentration, minimum fungicidal concentration, and mechanistic studies are still needed to validate the antifungal potential. Discover more Read Med Journals Find an OBGYN Study Biology On the computational side, the researchers docked HIHPT into the SARS-CoV-2 main protease, Mpro, using the Glide Standard Precision protocol in the Schrödinger Suite after validating the protocol by re-docking the co-crystallized ligand, methyl 4-sulfamoylbenzoate, with a root-mean-square deviation below 1.0 angstrom. HIHPT achieved a docking score of −5.913 kcal/mol and a binding energy of −45.525 kcal/mol, comparable to the reference ligand’s −6.518 kcal/mol and −47.112 kcal/mol. The docked pose formed two hydrogen bonds with Glu166 and Pro168, residues involved in substrate recognition and inhibitor stabilization, plus hydrophobic alkyl and pi-alkyl contacts with Met49 and Met165 in the S2 subsite. These docking results indicate a stable predicted binding conformation but do not by themselves demonstrate antiviral efficacy. Molecular dynamics simulations extended the docking analysis over 100 nanoseconds for two systems: the protease bound to the positive control compound Z18197050 and the protease bound to HIHPT. The root-mean-square deviation of C-alpha atoms settled near 2.4 angstroms for the control system and about 2.0 angstroms for the HIHPT complex, suggesting both systems equilibrated without major conformational change in the protease. Residues in contact with either ligand fluctuated by less than 6.0 angstroms. Because the simulation was implicit-solvent, water-mediated hydrogen-bonded interactions appeared with Glu166, Val186, Arg188, Gln189, Thr190, and Gln192 for the control, and with His41, Ser46, Asn142, Glu146, Gln189, and Thr190 for HIHPT, with Gln189 and Thr190 common to both complexes. Hydrophobic contacts involved Met49 and Met165 for the control and Met65 and Pro168 for the extracted compound. MM-GBSA binding free energy calculations on twenty snapshots taken at 5-nanosecond intervals showed consistently negative energies for both complexes. The control ranged from approximately −16.93 to −42.96 kcal/mol, with strain-corrected values from −17.37 to −44.01 kcal/mol, while HIHPT ranged from about −22.73 to −38.27 kcal/mol, or −23.73 to −39.01 kcal/mol with strain correction. The control generally bound more favorably, particularly near the end of the trajectory, but HIHPT maintained stable interaction energies throughout without significant fluctuations, and the small 1 to 3 kcal/mol differences between corrected and uncorrected values indicated minimal ligand conformational strain. The authors interpret this as thermodynamically favorable binding that warrants further biological validation rather than as evidence of inhibition. Additional quantum chemical and property calculations rounded out the profile. Density functional theory at the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) level yielded a HOMO-LUMO gap of 6.632 electron volts for HIHPT, close to the two reference ligands, with frontier orbitals localized on the cyclic portion of the molecule. Natural bond orbital charges identified the hydroxyl oxygen atoms as the most negative sites and hydroxyl hydrogens as the most positive, consistent with the molecular electrostatic potential map. Online property predictors estimated a cLogP near 5.3, no predicted mutagenicity, tumorigenicity, irritation, or reproductive toxicity risks, a drug-likeness score of −2.42, and a drug score of 0.21. A calculated intrinsic log P of 4.56 and intrinsic solubility of −4.85 log mol/L indicated a strongly lipophilic, poorly water-soluble neutral molecule that remains largely non-ionized between pH 1 and 12, which the authors note may limit aqueous dissolution and oral bioavailability absent formulation strategies. Taken together, the study positions HIHPT as a natural lead compound whose measured antifungal activity against clinical Candida isolates and predicted binding to SARS-CoV-2 Mpro justify further investigation. The authors themselves frame the conclusion cautiously: in vitro assays, docking, dynamics simulations, and property analyses revealed favorable biological activity, stable target interactions, and acceptable drug-like characteristics, but in vivo studies and clinical investigations are required to validate therapeutic efficacy and safety. For now, the findings add to the documented chemical diversity of Saharan medicinal flora and illustrate how traditional-use plants can yield structurally interesting triterpenoids for modern screening pipelines, while the gap between a laboratory inhibition zone and a clinically useful medicine remains substantial. content: News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Insights Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event SUBSCRIBE Menu SUBSCRIBE Show Search News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Insights Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event Search Query Submit Search Press Releases SEKISUI Diagnostics Announces 510(k) Clearance and Launch of the OSOM® COVID-19/Flu A&B Combo Test October 28, 2026 | 2 min read Twitter LinkedIn Facebook Email Print SAN DIEGO, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SEKISUI Diagnostics, a global medical diagnostics manufacturer, has announced the launch of a 510(k) cleared rapid test to detect COVID-19 and Flu A&B in professional healthcare settings. The OSOM® COVID-19/Flu A&B Combo Test is a lateral flow immunochromatographic assay intended for the qualitative detection and differentiation of influenza A and influenza B nucleoprotein antigens and SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antigen directly in anterior nasal swab specimens from individuals with signs and symptoms of respiratory tract infection. CLIA-waived for point-of-care use, the OSOM COVID-19/Flu A&B Combo Test is manufactured in the USA and backed by an experienced technical services team of medical laboratory professionals. The OSOM COVID-19/Flu A&B Combo Test includes QC Inside®, a unique feature which maximizes the value of every kit by eliminating separate Quality Control (QC) costs and provides two additional patient tests for external QC at no charge. "With the Emergency Use Authorization ending, we know it is extremely important to continue to supply the market with the tools needed to diagnose respiratory infections quickly and accurately. We are pleased to be able to offer new customers and transition existing customers to a 510(k) cleared alternative as we enter the season, so they are well prepared before the termination takes effect." said Erica Blight, VP Strategy & Growth. As COVID-19 and influenza continue to present with overlapping symptoms, multiplex testing provides the advantage of identifying and differentiating multiple respiratory viruses from a single patient sample, helping support timely clinical decisions. SEKISUI Diagnostics is a well-known provider of many rapid diagnostic solutions to the professional and home testing markets through a portfolio of tests under the OSOM and Metrix® brands. About SEKISUI Diagnostics: With over 40 years of experience, SEKISUI Diagnostics' mission is to provide intelligent solutions to enhance life with science and improve the health of all people. We supply innovative medical diagnostics globally to physicians, hospitals, laboratories and alternate testing locations. Our product lines include clinical chemistry reagents, point-of-care tests, pre-analytic systems, contract design and manufacturing as well as enzymes and specialty biochemicals. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 1, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Immune Complexes of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and Nucleocapsid Drive Inflammation by October 29, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Immune Complexes of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and Nucleocapsid Drive Inflammation Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Immune complexes built from SARS-CoV-2 RNA, the viral nucleocapsid protein and anti-nucleocapsid IgG1 antibodies can drive the runaway inflammation seen in severe COVID-19, according to a laboratory study published in PLOS Pathogens. Researchers found that when these RNA-containing complexes are taken up by primary human monocytes, the cells produce inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in a response that depends on Fcγ receptors and is partially dependent on toll-like receptor 8. The team, led by Johannes S. Gach and colleagues, traced how this phagocytic uptake translates into tissue damage. When monocytes were stimulated with the RNA-containing immune complexes, the inflammatory response they mounted caused endothelial dysfunction in vascularized micro-organs, laboratory models of human blood vessels. This links antibody-assisted clearance of viral material to a hallmark of severe disease: injury to the vascular lining. The study also addressed where such complexes come from. Using nasopharyngeal samples from SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals, the researchers captured SARS-CoV-2 RNA and nucleocapsid protein with an anti-nucleocapsid monoclonal antibody without using lysing reagents. That result indicates the RNA and nucleocapsid complexes exist outside of virions and cells in the airways, making them available to form inflammatory immune complexes with circulating antibodies. Discover more Study Biology Find Treatments Get Health Tips Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Consistent with a role for IgG-mediated inflammatory clearance in disease severity, the authors report that during an early wave of COVID-19, higher anti-nucleocapsid IgG:IgM ratios were associated with more severe clinical outcomes. They suggest this pattern fits a model in which inflammatory, IgG-driven phagocytic clearance of nucleic acid-containing immune complexes contributes to pathogenesis, while non-inflammatory, IgM-mediated clearance might mitigate it. As an observational association from one early pandemic wave, this finding supports but does not prove that mechanism. The authors conclude that RNA-containing immune complexes may play a role in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19. Because all pathogenic viruses encode nucleic acid-binding proteins similar to nucleocapsid, and these proteins often elicit antibody responses, they propose that inflammatory clearance of nucleic acid-containing immune complexes could also contribute to severity in other viral infections. As the work relies on in vitro monocyte assays, micro-organ models and patient sample analyses rather than direct clinical intervention studies, the findings define a plausible inflammatory mechanism and generate hypotheses for future research into severe viral disease rather than establishing treatment effects. Subject of Research: How SARS-CoV-2 RNA-containing immune complexes drive inflammatory cytokine production and endothelial dysfunction in severe COVID-19. (KATU) — Federal prosecutors in Oregon have recovered nearly $16 million as part of an ongoing crackdown on COVID-19 relief fraud, and officials say that number could grow significantly by the end of the year. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, federal officials are preparing to send thousands of demand letters to people whose COVID-19 relief loans showed potential signs of fraud. “Over the next few days, over 2,300 demand letters totaling nearly $97 million are being sent to applicants whose loans included indicators of fraud,” Inspector General William Kirk said. The letters seek repayment of funds associated with potentially fraudulent loans, although the $97 million has not yet been recovered. U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford said investigators have continued uncovering new cases in recent weeks. “Because it's still happening. That's 10 more cases, $34 million in losses and $7.2 million in recovery in just the last 45 days,” Bradford said. The DOJ is also working directly with the Internal Revenue Service to identify additional suspected fraud cases across Oregon. Officials say they have already received thousands of tips related to suspected fraud in the state, helping investigators identify potential cases. Kirk emphasized that the investigations are about recovering taxpayer money and preventing future fraud. “It's your money. These are taxpayer dollars that have been stolen from you, the taxpayer. And anything that we can recover and anything that we can deter going forward, any behavior like that going forward is gonna be to your benefit,” Kirk said. Federal officials say they will continue pursuing suspected fraud and recovering federal relief funds as investigations move forward. content: 24/7 LiveChicago & Suburban Cook Co.North SuburbsWest SuburbsSouth SuburbsNW Indiana 60° COVID 19 Chicago unveils COVID-19 memorial monument and park in Illinois Medical District It's located near Polk Street, Ogden Avenue and Damen Avenue in the Illinois Medical District. ByEvelyn Holmes Tuesday, October 27, 2026 5:16PM Share Follow ABC7 on Google CHICAGO (WLS) -- City leaders, health care workers and community members gathered on the West Side for the official unveiling of the COVID-19 Memorial Monument. ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch The monument and park were designed as a place for reflection and healing. It's located near the intersection of Polk Street, Ogden Avenue and Damen Avenue. The site, once a vacant space, was transformed into a tribute in the center of the Illinois Medical District, which was established in 1941. The project was made possible through $4.95 million in funding and grant support. "This is your park, come often, find a moment of peace and make it your own," said Allyson Hansen, chief executive officer and executive director of the Illinois Medical District Commission. Top Stories All 9 people died on jet that crashed into Florida neighborhood, transportation secretary says 28 minutes ago Woman shot to death in Oak Park, police say Other women contacted police about previous incidents with Packers' Josh Jacobs after his arrest 3 hours ago For many attendees, the ceremony served as recognition of a period marked by grief and hardship. The monument, designed to symbolize community resilience, is the result of more than a year of work by the COVID-19 Monument Commission. A Chicago-based volunteer-led initiative dedicated to honoring those who died during the pandemic while recognizing the contributions of essential workers. Following an international competition, the commission selected a design featuring illuminated stainless steel dandelion sculptures intended to symbolize remembrance, hope and renewal. It’s located near Polk Street, Ogden Avenue and Damen Avenue in the Illinois Medical District. Organizers said they hope the memorial monument and park will serve as a sacred space for generations to come, helping ensure that the lessons of the pandemic and the lost lives are not forgotten. content_title: Understanding the latest COVID strain
content: Understanding the latest COVID strain AS we move into the colder months, COVID-19 is once again attracting attention with reports of a variant being referred to in the media as 'American COVID'. For many people the pandemic may feel like a distant memory but coronavirus continues to circulate, evolve and occasionally cause serious illness. So what is this new strain, how does it affect us and what can we do to protect ourselves and our families? The variant attracting attention is known as XFG, also called Stratus. It belongs to the Omicron family of coronavirus variants and was first identified in January 2025. It has subsequently spread internationally and been detected in the UK. The term 'American COVID' is somewhat misleading. It does not mean that the virus originated in America or that it is confined to the United States. The nickname reflects its association with the country where it was first identified in media coverage. XFG has genetic changes that may help it evade some immunity acquired through previous infection or vaccination. This may contribute to its ability to spread. However, there is currently no convincing evidence that XFG causes more severe illness than other circulating variants. The UK Health Security Agency continues to monitor its behaviour and the wider impact of COVID-19. COVID-19 spreads predominantly through the air. Infected individuals release respiratory particles when breathing, speaking, coughing or sneezing. Transmission is particularly likely in crowded, poorly ventilated indoor environments. People can spread the virus before developing symptoms and some infections remain asymptomatic. The clinical presentation of the current variants is generally similar to that of previous Omicron strains. Common symptoms include a sore throat, fever, chills, cough, runny nose, nasal congestion, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, nausea, diarrhoea or changes in taste and smell. Symptoms may initially resemble a common cold or influenza. Most people experience a mild illness and recover without needing hospital treatment. Nevertheless, older people, pregnant women, individuals with weakened immune systems and those with underlying conditions such as heart disease, diabetes or chronic lung disease remain particularly vulnerable to complications. For most otherwise healthy people, treatment involves rest, adequate fluids and appropriate medicines to relieve symptoms, such as paracetamol when needed. However, people at increased risk of severe illness should seek medical advice promptly if they develop symptoms. Antiviral treatments, including Paxlovid, may be appropriate for eligible patients, particularly when started early. These medicines require clinical assessment because they can interact with other medications. Severe COVID-19 can cause pneumonia, respiratory failure, blood clots and damage to organs. Although uncommon, these complications can be life-threatening. Another important consequence is long COVID in which symptoms persist for weeks or months after the initial infection. These may include exhaustion, breathlessness, muscle pain and difficulty concentrating, sometimes significantly affecting a person's ability to work or undertake everyday activities. Vaccination remains one of our most effective measures against severe COVID-19, hospitalisation and death. Although vaccines may not completely prevent infection, they help reduce the risk of serious illness. Eligible individuals, particularly older adults and people with underlying medical conditions, should follow current NHS vaccination advice. Simple measures also make a difference. Staying at home when unwell, improving ventilation, washing hands regularly and wearing a well-fitting mask in crowded indoor spaces when appropriate can reduce transmission. If symptoms develop, consider testing, particularly if you are vulnerable or live with someone at increased risk. The emergence of another coronavirus variant should remind us that COVID-19 has not disappeared. However, the available evidence does not suggest that the American COVID variant represents a return to the early days of the pandemic. We now have vaccines, treatments, improved clinical understanding and experience of managing respiratory infections. For Worcester and the surrounding communities, the message is straightforward — remain informed, take sensible precautions, protect those most vulnerable and seek medical advice when necessary. COVID-19 is now part of our continuing public health landscape. With awareness and proportionate action, we can reduce its impact while continuing to live our lives. Our columnist Dr Jason Seewoodhary is a former Worcestershire GP
